steps.title: Filter extreme outliers
steps.description: Decide whether to retain or winsorize extreme values in balance, duration, campaign, pdays, and previous.

options.label: Winsorize extreme values at 1st and 99th percentiles
options.rationale: Reduces influence of extreme outliers while retaining all observations; appropriate for highly skewed variables like balance and previous.
options.spec: For each column in ['balance', 'duration', 'campaign', 'pdays', 'previous'], compute the 1st and 99th percentiles; replace values below the 1st percentile with the 1st percentile value and above the 99th percentile with the 99th percentile value; return the modified DataFrame.

options.label: Exclude rows with extreme outliers
options.rationale: Removes observations with extreme values that may unduly influence estimates; appropriate if outliers are believed to be errors or from a different population.
options.spec: For each column in ['balance', 'duration', 'campaign', 'pdays', 'previous'], compute the 1st and 99th percentiles; exclude rows where any column value is below the 1st or above the 99th percentile; return the filtered DataFrame.

steps.title: Handle missing values
steps.description: Decide how to handle missing values in job, education, contact, and poutcome.

options.label: Missing indicator method
options.rationale: Preserves sample size and allows missingness to be informative; creates binary indicators for missingness and imputes missing values with a placeholder.
options.spec: For each column in ['job', 'education', 'contact', 'poutcome']: create a new column '{col}_missing' (1 if original is null, else 0); fill nulls in original column with 'missing'; return DataFrame with original and new columns.

options.label: Exclude rows with any missing values
options.rationale: Complete case analysis; avoids model assumptions about missing data mechanism but may introduce bias if missing not completely at random.
options.spec: Drop rows where any of ['job', 'education', 'contact', 'poutcome'] is null; return the filtered DataFrame.

steps.title: Estimate odds ratio per additional call
steps.description: Estimate the odds ratio of subscribing per additional contact call using logistic regression with different covariance estimators.

options.label: Logistic regression with conventional standard errors
options.rationale: Standard maximum likelihood logistic regression assuming independent observations; appropriate starting point for inference.
options.spec: Fit a logistic regression model with statsmodels.Logit where y is the dependent variable, campaign is the focal predictor, and ctx['covariates'] are covariates (each string-categorical column is encoded with drop_first=True); use ordinary covariance; return fitted model.

options.label: Logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors
options.rationale: Accounts for potential clustering of residuals by job category (or other meaningful groups) to avoid underestimated standard errors; job has 11 levels, suitable for clustering.
options.spec: Fit the same logistic regression model as in opt4a but compute cluster-robust covariance matrix using job as the cluster variable; return fitted model with clustered standard errors. (opt4a: Fit a logistic regression model with statsmodels.Logit where y is the dependent variable, campaign is the focal predictor, and ctx['covariates'] are covariates (each string-categorical column is encoded with drop_first=True); use ordinary covariance; return fitted model.)

data.reason: Cluster-robust SEs by job category address within-group correlation without altering the point estimate; appropriate given 11 job levels and potential residual dependence.
Excluding outlier rows reduces sample size arbitrarily and can bias the odds ratio if outliers are valid but rare cases; winsorizing preserves information while limiting influence.
Complete-case analysis risks selection bias unless data are MCAR; here missingness likely depends on observed variables like job or education, making it questionable without stronger justification.
Adding contact timing and prior campaign variables addresses confounding without introducing post-treatment bias; excluding poutcome and duration aligns with causal principles.

Mode imputation within marital subgroups risks introducing bias because marital status may be associated with both missingness and the outcome, potentially distorting the exposure-outcome relationship without sufficient justification.

Retaining raw predictor values is a reasonable alternative; while winsorizing can improve robustness, omitting it does not introduce severe bias here because logistic regression is relatively insensitive to moderate outliers and the sample size is large.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def apply(df, ctx):
    cols = ['balance', 'duration', 'campaign', 'pdays', 'previous']
    for col in cols:
        p1 = df[col].quantile(0.01)
        p99 = df[col].quantile(0.99)
        df[col] = df[col].clip(lower=p1, upper=p99)
    return df

steps.title: Estimate odds ratio per additional call
steps.description: Estimate the odds ratio of subscribing per additional contact call using logistic regression with different covariance estimators.

options.label: Logistic regression with conventional standard errors
options.rationale: Standard maximum likelihood logistic regression assuming independent observations; appropriate starting point for inference.
options.spec: Fit a logistic regression model with statsmodels.Logit where y is the dependent variable, campaign is the focal predictor, and ctx['covariates'] are covariates (each string-categorical column is encoded with drop_first=True); use ordinary covariance; return fitted model.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = [] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(names) if c not in ['y', 'campaign']]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['y', 'campaign'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    finite = [c for c in used if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    data = data[np.isfinite(data[finite].astype(float)).all(axis=1)]
    if len(data) and data['campaign'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'campaign' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['campaign']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['y'].astype(float)
    model = sm.Logit(endog, exog)
    fit = model.fit(disp=0, cov_type="nonrobust")
    term = 'campaign'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(value)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(low)),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(high)),
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
        "extra": {"coefficient": value},
    }

option.label: Include interaction between campaign and duration
option.rationale: Duration may modify the effect of campaign calls; adding an interaction tests whether the marginal effect of each additional call varies by call length, which could attenuate the main effect toward null.
option.spec: Create a new column 'campaign_duration' = campaign * duration; set ctx['covariates'] = ['job', 'marital', 'education', 'default', 'housing', 'loan', 'campaign_duration']; return DataFrame with the new column.

option.label: Firth's penalized logistic regression to reduce small-sample bias
option.rationale: Firth's regression reduces bias in logistic regression estimates, especially with rare events or high-dimensional covariates, which may pull the odds ratio toward 1 (null), opposing the baseline significant protective effect.
option.spec: Use statsmodels' Logit with method='bfgs' and add a Jeffreys prior penalty via fit_regularized(L1_wt=0, alpha=1) to approximate Firth's penalized logistic regression; keep same covariates and encoding as opt4a; return fitted model.

option.label: Trim extreme values at 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles for campaign only
option.rationale: Trimming only the campaign variable at more extreme thresholds reduces influence of ultra-high contact counts without altering other variables, potentially weakening the estimated effect if high campaign values drive the baseline result.
option.spec: For the column 'campaign', compute the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles; replace values below the 0.5th percentile with the 0.5th percentile value and above the 99.5th percentile with the 99.5th percentile value; leave all other columns unchanged; return the modified DataFrame.

option.label: Delete rows with missing values in job, education, contact, or poutcome
option.rationale: Complete case analysis may yield a different estimate if missingness is related to both campaign and outcome; if missing cases have weaker campaign effects, removing them could attenuate the observed association.
option.spec: Drop any row where job, education, contact, or poutcome is null; return the resulting DataFrame with no additional columns.

data.reason: Including duration creates a post-treatment confounder because duration occurs after campaign exposure and can be affected by it, introducing bias into the odds ratio estimate.
Complete-case analysis risks bias if missingness depends on unobserved factors related to exposure or outcome; without evidence MCAR holds, it is not a defensible default.
Firth's penalized logistic regression is a recognized alternative to reduce small-sample bias in logistic regression, particularly with rare events or separation, without changing the estimand.
Trimming only the exposure variable at more extreme thresholds is a reasonable sensitivity check to assess robustness of the odds ratio estimate to influential outliers in campaign calls.

steps.title: Filter extreme outliers
steps.description: Decide whether to retain or winsorize extreme values in balance, duration, campaign, pdays, and previous.

options.label: Winsorize extreme values at 1st and 99th percentiles
options.rationale: Reduces influence of extreme outliers while retaining all observations; appropriate for highly skewed variables like balance and previous.
options.spec: For each column in ['balance', 'duration', 'campaign', 'pdays', 'previous'], compute the 1st and 99th percentiles; replace values below the 1st percentile with the 1st percentile value and above the 99th percentile with the 99th percentile value; return the modified DataFrame.
options.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def apply(df, ctx):
    cols = ['balance', 'duration', 'campaign', 'pdays', 'previous']
    for col in cols:
        p1 = df[col].quantile(0.01)
        p99 = df[col].quantile(0.99)
        df[col] = df[col].clip(lower=p1, upper=p99)
    return df

options.label: No filtering or transformation of variables
options.rationale: Retaining all data without modification avoids arbitrary decisions about what constitutes an outlier and prevents potential bias from altering the distribution of predictors; the logistic regression model is robust to mild outliers due to its bounded outcome.
options.spec: Return the input DataFrame unchanged; no modifications to balance, duration, campaign, pdays, or previous.
options.source: Hosmer Jr et al., Applied Logistic Regression, 3rd ed., Wiley 2013, sec. 4.2.3

options.label: Trim extreme values at 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles for campaign only
options.rationale: Trimming only the campaign variable at more extreme thresholds reduces influence of ultra-high contact counts without altering other variables, potentially weakening the estimated effect if high campaign values drive the baseline result.
options.spec: For the column 'campaign', compute the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles; replace values below the 0.5th percentile with the 0.5th percentile value and above the 99.5th percentile with the 99.5th percentile value; leave all other columns unchanged; return the modified DataFrame.
options.code:
import pandas as pd

def apply(df, ctx):
    q_low = df['campaign'].quantile(0.005)
    q_high = df['campaign'].quantile(0.995)
    df = df.copy()
    df.loc[df['campaign'] < q_low, 'campaign'] = q_low
    df.loc[df['campaign'] > q_high, 'campaign'] = q_high
    return df

steps.title: Estimate odds ratio per additional call
steps.description: Estimate the odds ratio of subscribing per additional contact call using logistic regression with different covariance estimators.

options.label: Logistic regression with conventional standard errors
options.rationale: Standard maximum likelihood logistic regression assuming independent observations; appropriate starting point for inference.
options.spec: Fit a logistic regression model with statsmodels.Logit where y is the dependent variable, campaign is the focal predictor, and ctx['covariates'] are covariates (each string-categorical column is encoded with drop_first=True); use ordinary covariance; return fitted model.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = [] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(names) if c not in ['y', 'campaign']]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['y', 'campaign'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    finite = [c for c in used if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    data = data[np.isfinite(data[finite].astype(float)).all(axis=1)]
    if len(data) and data['campaign'].nunique() < 2:
        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'campaign' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['campaign']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)
        floor = 1e-07 * (float(np.abs(target).max()) or 1.0)
        involved = [c for c, size in zip(kept, sizes) if size > floor]
        if any(c in core.columns for c in involved):
            tangled += [c for c in involved if c not in protected]
    tangled = list(dict.fromkeys(tangled))
    exog = exog.drop(columns=aliased + tangled)
    note = 'aliased covariates dropped: ' + ', '.join(aliased) if aliased else ''
    note += '; covariates that rebuild the exposure with them dropped: ' + ', '.join(tangled) if tangled else ''
    endog = data['y'].astype(float)
    model = sm.Logit(endog, exog)
    fit = model.fit(disp=0, cov_type="nonrobust")
    term = 'campaign'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(value)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(low)),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(high)),
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "note": note,
        "extra": {"coefficient": value},
    }

options.label: Logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors
options.rationale: Accounts for potential clustering of residuals by job category (or other meaningful groups) to avoid underestimated standard errors; job has 11 levels, suitable for clustering.
options.spec: Fit the same logistic regression model as in opt4a but compute cluster-robust covariance matrix using job as the cluster variable; return fitted model with clustered standard errors. (opt4a: Fit a logistic regression model with statsmodels.Logit where y is the dependent variable, campaign is the focal predictor, and ctx['covariates'] are covariates (each string-categorical column is encoded with drop_first=True); use ordinary covariance; return fitted model.)

import numpy as np

        raise ValueError('the exposure ' + 'campaign' + ' has the same value in every row, so it is collinear with the intercept and its effect cannot be estimated: the earlier step that builds it produced a constant. A threshold taken from a numpy median, percentile or quantile is NaN when the column has missing values, and no row then passes it. The pandas median and quantile methods skip missing values')
    core = data[['campaign']].astype(float)

    if other:

        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    labels = pd.Series(exog.columns.map(str))
    repeats = labels.groupby(labels).cumcount()
    exog.columns = [f'{c}_repeat{n}' if n else c for c, n in zip(labels, repeats)]
    protected = ['const', *map(str, core.columns)]
    basis = np.zeros((len(exog), 0))
    aliased = []
    for column in list(exog.columns):
        vector = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(vector))
        residual = vector / size if size else vector
        for _ in range(2):
            residual = residual - basis @ (basis.T @ residual)
        size = float(np.linalg.norm(residual))
        if size >= 1e-07:
            basis = np.column_stack([basis, residual / size])
        elif str(column) not in protected:
            aliased.append(str(column))
    kept = [c for c in exog.columns if c not in aliased]
    tangled = []
    for column in aliased:
        target = exog[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        weights = np.linalg.lstsq(exog[kept].to_numpy(dtype=float), target, rcond=None)[0]
        sizes = np.abs(weights) * exog[kept].abs().max().to_numpy(dtype=float)

influences.title: Estimate odds ratio per additional call

report.robustness_design_note: uniform random sample of the grid: 12 draws (each decision picks each of its options equally), 8 distinct results; independent of the beam search

estimand_changes.label: Extended adjustment: add contact, day_of_week, month, pdays, previous
estimand_changes.detail: changes the covariates of the model (adds contact, contact_missing, day_of_week, month, pdays, previous): adjusting for another set of covariates answers a different conditional question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity

report.narrative: The original analysis estimated 0.872 (95% CI 0.857 to 0.886, p < 0.001, n = 45,211) and returned the verdict CAP THE CALLS. No minimal flip was found; no combination of defensible analytic changes reversed the verdict. The judge accepted three alternatives: retaining raw predictor values without outlier filtering (defensibility 0.7), using cluster-robust standard errors by job category (defensibility 0.85), and extending the covariate set to include contact timing, day of week, month, days since last contact, and previous campaign outcome (defensibility 0.8). The judge rejected excluding outlier rows, complete-case analysis for missing values, and mode imputation within marital subgroups. Across 12 explored universes, the odds ratio ranged from 0.872 to 0.903, with all confidence intervals remaining entirely below 1.0. The extended covariate adjustment produced the largest shift, moving the estimate from 0.872 to 0.896–0.903 depending on outlier handling. Outlier filtering choices shifted the estimate by up to 0.006. Cluster-robust standard errors left the point estimate unchanged but widened confidence intervals. Robustness: 100% of the analysis grid agrees with the original verdict and 0% reverses it.
caveats: Robustness headline: 100% of the analysis grid agrees with the original verdict (uniform random sample of the grid: 12 draws (each decision picks each of its options equally), 8 distinct results; independent of the beam search). Among the universes the search explored, 100% agree, but the beam search samples the universes that are closest to flipping, so that share leans toward flips.
